items.title: The Spread of Roman Citizenship, 14–212 CE: Quantification in the Face of High Uncertainty
items.note: Models growth of the citizen body from the 14 CE census total, making explicit how the reading of the Augustan figures carries into later estimates.

items.title: The Population of Roman Italy in Town and Country
items.venue: Reconstructing Past Population Trends in Mediterranean Europe (Oxbow)
items.note: Restates the case for a larger Italian population by weighing urban and rural evidence against the rival readings of the census totals.

items.title: An Urban Geography of the Roman World, 100 BC to AD 300
items.note: Catalogue of some 1,400 Roman urban sites with area estimates, giving an empire-wide basis for urban population figures in Italy.

items.title: Something Old, Something New: Social and Economic Developments in the Countryside of Roman Italy between Republic and Empire
items.venue: The Economic Integration of Roman Italy (Brill)
items.note: Uses field-survey site counts to trace rural settlement across the late Republic and early Empire, a test of the decline implied by the low count.

items.title: The Changing Landscapes of Rome's Northern Hinterland: The British School at Rome's Tiber Valley Project
items.who: H. Patterson, R. Witcher and H. Di Giuseppe
items.note: Final synthesis of the restudy of the South Etruria Survey and related data, a database of about 5,000 sites.

items.title: A Method for Estimating Roman Population Sizes from Urban Survey Contexts: An Application in Central Adriatic Italy
items.who: D. Van Limbergen and F. Vermeulen
items.note: Proposes a procedure for turning intensive urban survey data into town population estimates, applied to towns of central Adriatic Italy.

items.title: The Roman Hinterland Project: Integrating Archaeological Field Surveys around Rome and Beyond
items.who: P. A. J. Attema, P. Carafa, W. M. Jongman, C. J. Smith et al.
items.note: Harmonizes several survey datasets around Rome into a common database, the integration needed to test rural population models against the census.

items.title: The Census
items.venue: A Companion to the Political Culture of the Roman Republic (Wiley)
items.note: Overview of the Republican census as a political and administrative institution, including who registered and how totals were produced.

items.title: Integration and Self-Integration of Foreigners in the Roman Census during the Roman Republic
items.venue: Understanding Integration in the Roman World (Brill)
items.note: Examines how non-citizens entered the census rolls, legitimately or not, a factor in reading growth between Republican and Augustan totals.

items.title: Cives Romanae: Roman Women as Citizens during the Republic
items.note: Nineteen studies of women's civic status and public roles, background to whether and how women entered the citizen count.

items.title: Censimenti romani e demografia: ritorno alle fonti
items.venue: Quaderni Lupiensi di Storia e Diritto
items.note: Re-reads the sources on cives sine suffragio, the Gracchan period and census decentralization, concluding that fourth- to first-century figures fit the low count.

items.title: Women and the Census in the Roman Republic
items.venue: Women, Wealth and Power in the Roman Republic (Cambridge University Press)
items.note: Examines how women figured in Republican census registration, the question on which the jump in the Augustan totals largely turns.
